q: reset() assigns a brand new array to its parameter. What does main print?
options: Compile error: a parameter cannot be reassigned
why: Java passes a copy of the reference. Inside reset(), arr is a local copy; pointing it at a new array changes only that copy. The caller's a still refers to the original {5, 7}.
wrong: That would need pass-by-reference. Reassigning the parameter never reaches the caller's variable.
Nothing is written into the original array, so neither element changes.
Parameters are ordinary local variables and can be reassigned unless they are declared final.

q: addGuest() calls add() on the list it receives. What does main print?
options: [ann]
[bo]
Compile error: the list is not returned
[ann, bo]
why: The method gets a copy of the reference, and that copy points to the same list object as the caller's variable. Calling add() changes the shared object, so the caller sees the new item.
wrong: The method does not need to return the list; it changed the very object the caller holds.
add() appends; it does not replace the existing item.
A void method can change an object it receives; nothing has to be returned for that.

q: A method receives an int n and a Counter object c. It runs n++ and c.value++. After it returns, which change does the caller see?
options: Only c.value; n was a copy of the number
Both changes, since both were passed in
Neither change, since Java copies every argument
Only n, since objects are copied into the method
why: Everything is passed by value. For n the value is the number itself, so the method works on its own copy. For c the value is a reference, so the copy still points to the caller's object, and c.value++ changes that object.
wrong: A primitive is copied, so n++ only changes the method's local copy.
The reference is copied, not the object, so changes made through it reach the shared object.
Objects are never copied when passed; only the reference to them is.

q: This swap() is meant to exchange the caller's two strings. What does main print?
options: right left
left left
left right
Compile error: strings are immutable
why: x and y are copies of the caller's references. The method swaps its own copies and then returns, so a and b in main still point where they did. A swap method cannot reassign the caller's variables in Java.
wrong: That would need pass-by-reference; swapping local copies does not touch a and b.
No assignment ever reaches a or b, so neither is overwritten.
The code only reassigns variables; it never tries to change a String object, so it compiles.

q: update() first appends to the builder it receives, then points its parameter at a new builder and appends again. What does main print?
options: a1
x2
a
why: The first append runs on the caller's object, so it becomes a1. After sb = new StringBuilder("x"), the parameter points to a different object, and the second append changes only that one, which is then dropped.
wrong: After the reassignment, sb no longer refers to the caller's builder, so 2 goes elsewhere.
The caller's variable is never redirected; only the method's copy of the reference is.
The first append happened through a shared reference, before the reassignment, so it is kept.

q: Two String methods are called on s, but their results are not stored. What does this print?
options: java
JAVA
javascript
JAVAscript
why: A String can never change after it is created. toUpperCase() and concat() build new strings and return them; since the results are thrown away, s still refers to the original java.
wrong: toUpperCase() returns a new string; it does not change s.
concat() also returns a new string and leaves s as it was.
Neither call changes s, and their results were never assigned to anything.

q: a is a string literal and b is built with new String. What does this print?
options: true true
true false
false true
false false
why: == checks whether two references point to the same object. new String always creates a separate object, so a == b is false. equals() compares the characters, which match, so it is true.
wrong: == does not compare text; the two variables point to different objects.
This mixes up the two: == is the identity check and equals() is the text check.
String overrides equals() to compare characters, so equal text gives true.

q: role == "admin" passed every unit test, where role was a literal. In production, role is read from a file and holds exactly the text admin, yet the check fails. Why?
options: Text read from a file ends with hidden spaces or a newline, and == cannot ignore them
== works only on strings shorter than a fixed length
The file was saved in another character encoding, so the characters really differ
== compares objects; equal literals share one, but file text is a new object
why: Identical string literals in a program are stored once and shared, so the test compared one object with itself. A string read at run time is a new object, so == is false even with the same text. Use equals() for text.
wrong: Spaces would break equals() too. Here the text is the same and only the objects differ.
Length has nothing to do with it; == never compares characters at all.
The text matches. The failure comes from comparing objects instead of contents.

q: A loop runs s += word for thousands of words. A reviewer asks for a StringBuilder instead. What does that change?
options: Nothing: the compiler already turns the whole loop into one single concatenation
Each += copies all text so far into a new String; a builder appends to one buffer
+= changes s in place, but it locks the string on every pass, which is what makes it slow
StringBuilder skips Unicode checks, so each character is cheaper
why: Because strings are immutable, each += creates a new String holding a copy of everything built so far, and the old one becomes garbage. A StringBuilder keeps one growing buffer and appends to it, so earlier text is not copied again on every pass.
wrong: The compiler can join one expression, but it does not merge the separate += steps of a loop into one result.
Strings cannot change in place; the cost comes from building new ones, not from locking.
Both work with the same characters; the difference is copying, not Unicode handling.

q: String a = "x"; String b = a; a += "y"; runs. What does b hold now?
options: xy, because a and b share one String object
y, because += moves the text from a
x, because a now points to a new String
null, because the old String was released
why: a += "y" builds a new String xy and points a at it. The original x is untouched, and b still refers to it. With an immutable type, no other variable can see a change made through a.
wrong: They did share x, but += cannot change that object; it creates a new one for a only.
Nothing is moved; concatenation copies text into a new string.
b still refers to the x object, so it is reachable and stays as it is.

q: A list is read by index inside loops, like list.get(i), and new items are only added at the end. Which implementation fits, and why?
options: ArrayList: get(i) is a direct jump into an array
LinkedList: adding at the end is its strength
LinkedList: it uses less memory per item
Either one, since the List interface makes them cost the same
why: ArrayList stores items in an array, so get(i) goes straight to the slot, and adding at the end is cheap on average. A LinkedList must walk node by node to reach index i, which hurts inside a loop.
wrong: ArrayList also appends cheaply, and LinkedList pays O(i) for every get(i).
Each LinkedList node also stores links to its neighbours, so it usually uses more memory.
The interface is the same, but each class has its own cost for the same call.

q: Three fruit names are put into a TreeMap in this order. What does this print?
options: [pear, apple, fig]
[fig, pear, apple]
The keys in an unpredictable order
[apple, fig, pear]
why: A TreeMap keeps its keys sorted, here in alphabetical order for strings, whatever order they were inserted in. That is the main reason to choose it over a HashMap.
wrong: Insertion order is what a LinkedHashMap keeps, not a TreeMap.
Keys are not sorted by length; strings sort alphabetically.
No guaranteed order is the HashMap behaviour; a TreeMap is always sorted.

q: In tests, a HashMap printed its entries in the order they were inserted, so a report now depends on that order. Is that safe?
options: Yes: a HashMap keeps insertion order for small maps
No: HashMap promises no order; use LinkedHashMap to keep it
Yes, as long as no key is ever removed from the map
No: a HashMap shuffles its entries on purpose after each put
why: A HashMap orders entries by hash bucket, and that order can change as the map grows. Matching insertion order in a test was luck. LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order and TreeMap keeps sorted order by contract.
wrong: No size gives an order guarantee; small maps can look ordered by chance.
Order can change after inserts too, when the map resizes, not only after removals.
There is no deliberate shuffling; the order follows hashing and is simply not promised.

q: A list of emails has repeats, and you need each email once. Order does not matter. What is the simplest approach?
options: Sort the list first, because sorting removes repeated values as it orders them
Call list.distinct(), which every List has
Copy the list into a HashSet, which keeps one copy of each value
Use a TreeMap with the email as the value
why: A Set holds each value at most once, so new HashSet<>(list) drops the repeats in one step. HashSet relies on the String class's equals() and hashCode(), which compare text.
wrong: Sorting puts equal values next to each other but keeps all of them.
List has no such method; removing duplicates is what a Set is for.
Map values may repeat; only keys are unique, and the emails would still need to be keys.

q: The loop removes even numbers from the list it is iterating with for-each. What happens?
options: ConcurrentModificationException at run time
Compile error: a list cannot be changed inside for-each
why: A for-each loop uses an iterator, which notices that the list was changed behind its back and throws on its next step. To remove while iterating, call remove() on an explicit Iterator or use removeIf.
wrong: That is the intended result, but the iterator fails after the first removal.
The loop does not quietly skip ahead; the iterator throws as soon as it detects the change.
The compiler does not track this; the problem is only detected while the loop runs.

q: To avoid an exception, the loop now removes even numbers by index. What does this print?
options: IndexOutOfBoundsException at run time
why: Removing at index i shifts every later item left by one. When 2 is removed, 4 moves into index 0, but i moves on to 1, so 4 is never checked. 6 is then found and removed, leaving [4, 5].
wrong: That assumes every even number is checked, but the shift makes the loop skip the item after each removal.
The loop reads nums.size() on every pass, so i never goes past the end.
6 is still checked after the skip, and it is even, so it is removed.

q: days is created with List.of, then add() is called on it. What happens?
options: [mon, tue, wed]
UnsupportedOperationException at run time
Compile error: List.of returns a read-only type
[mon, tue], because the add is ignored
why: List.of returns an unmodifiable list. Its type is still List, so add() compiles, but the call throws when it runs. Copy it into new ArrayList<>(...) when you need a list you can change.
wrong: The list cannot grow; any change to it is rejected.
The declared type is plain List, which has add(), so the compiler accepts the call.
Changes are not silently dropped; the list throws so the mistake is visible.

q: What is the practical difference between a checked exception, such as IOException, and an unchecked one, such as NullPointerException?
options: Checked ones are checked by the JVM while the program runs; unchecked ones are never checked
Unchecked exceptions cannot be caught with try and catch
The compiler makes you catch or declare checked ones; unchecked ones usually mean a bug
Checked exceptions cannot stop the program, only unchecked ones can
why: Checked exceptions describe failures a correct program should expect, like a missing file, so the compiler forces callers to handle or declare them. Unchecked ones usually mean a coding error and need no declaration.
wrong: The checking is done by the compiler, not at run time. That is where the name comes from.
Any exception can be caught, including NullPointerException.
An uncaught checked exception ends a thread just as an unchecked one does.

q: load() returns from inside try, and its finally block prints a line. What does this program print?
options: cleanup, then data
data only
data, then cleanup
Compile error: code after return is unreachable
why: A finally block runs whenever control leaves the try, including through return. The return value is ready, finally prints cleanup, and then the method returns, so main prints data next.
wrong: finally is not skipped by return; that guarantee is the whole point of finally.
finally runs before the method actually returns, so its output comes first.
A finally block is not code after the return; it is part of how the try exits.

q: f() returns x from try, and finally then sets x to 2. What does this print?
options: Compile error: x is changed after the return
Nothing: the return skips the finally block
why: return x evaluates x first and keeps the value 1 as the result. finally then runs and sets the local x to 2, but the value already chosen to return is not read again, so 1 is printed.
wrong: finally does run, but it changes the variable, not the value already saved for the return.
A finally block may assign local variables; it compiles without problems.
finally always runs when the try exits, including through a return.

q: A FileNotFoundException is thrown. The catch for Exception comes before the catch for IOException. What happens?
options: general
io, because the most specific matching catch is always chosen
general, then io, since both catch blocks match
Compile error: the IOException catch can never be reached
why: Catch blocks are tried in order, and Exception already matches every IOException. The second block could never run, so the compiler rejects it. Put the more specific catch first.
wrong: That would be the run time result, but the code never compiles.
Order matters: the first matching catch wins, and Exception would match first.
At most one catch block runs for a thrown exception.

q: The resource's close() prints a line, and the try body throws. In what order are lines printed?
options: use, caught, close
use, close, caught
use, caught; close() is skipped because of the exception
use, then a crash, since the catch is never reached
why: try-with-resources closes the resource as soon as the try block exits, normally or by an exception. The resource is closed first, then the matching catch runs. That is why it is safer than closing by hand.
wrong: The catch belongs to the same statement, but the resource is closed before the catch runs.
Closing on an exception is exactly what try-with-resources guarantees.
The catch matches IllegalStateException, so the exception is handled after close().

q: A config parser wraps Integer.parseInt in try, has an empty catch, and returns 0 on failure. A timeout value is mistyped as 3O. What is the main problem?
options: The program still crashes, because an empty catch block does not handle anything
parseInt fixes the typo and reads it as 30
The error disappears: timeout silently becomes 0 with no message
The compiler rejects an empty catch block
why: Catching an exception and doing nothing hides it. The bad value turns into 0, nothing is logged, and the bug appears later somewhere else, such as requests timing out at once. Log it, rethrow it, or fail fast.
wrong: An empty catch handles the exception, so nothing crashes; that is the problem.
parseInt does not guess; the letter O makes it throw NumberFormatException.
An empty catch compiles; it is legal and therefore easy to get wrong.

q: A field is declared final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(). Which statement does the compiler reject?
options: names.add("x")
names.clear()
names = new ArrayList<>()
names.removeIf(s -> s.isEmpty())
why: final on a variable means it cannot be assigned again, so it always refers to the same list. It says nothing about the object itself, so methods that change the list are allowed.
wrong: add() changes the list, not the variable, so final does not stop it.
clear() changes the list's contents; the reference stays the same.
removeIf() is another change to the object, which final allows.

q: To make Point objects immutable, a teammate marks the class final. Point still has setX() and setY(). Is it immutable now?
options: No: final on a class only stops subclassing; the setters still change it
Yes: marking a class final also makes every one of its fields final automatically
Yes, but only for objects created after the change
No, because a final class cannot have setter methods
why: A final class cannot be extended, nothing more. Its fields can still be changed by its own methods. An immutable class also needs private final fields and no methods that modify state.
wrong: final on a class does not reach its fields; each field must be declared final itself.
Being final is a property of the class and does not affect how fields behave in any object.
A final class may have any methods, including setters, so the code compiles as it is.

q: count is an instance field, and static main uses it directly. What happens?
options: 1, because count starts at 0 and main increments it once before printing
Compile error: count belongs to an object, and static main has none
NullPointerException at run time, since no Main object exists yet
why: A static method belongs to the class and runs without any object, so there is no count to read. The compiler rejects it. Create an object first, such as new Main().count, or make count static.
wrong: main never gets an object, so there is no count field to increment.
The default value 0 belongs to an object's field, and no object exists here.
This is caught at compile time, so the program never runs.

q: The constructor's parameter has the same name as the field, and the body says balance = balance. What does this print?
options: Compile error: balance is declared twice
Compile error: a variable cannot be assigned to itself
why: Inside the constructor, the name balance refers to the parameter, which hides the field. The line assigns the parameter to itself, so the field keeps its default 0. this.balance = balance fixes it.
wrong: The field is never written; both sides of the assignment mean the parameter.
A parameter may share a field's name; it shadows the field instead of clashing.
Self-assignment is legal Java; the compiler accepts it, which is why the bug is easy to miss.

q: Inside a method, Point p = new Point(1, 2) runs. Where do the variable p and the Point object live?
options: p in the method's stack frame; the Point object on the heap
Both on the stack, since both are created inside the method's body
Both on the heap, since p refers to an object
p on the heap and the Point object on the stack
why: Local variables live in the method's stack frame and disappear when it returns. Objects created with new live on the heap, and p holds only a reference to one. The object can outlive the method if something else still refers to it.
wrong: Objects made with new go on the heap, wherever the code that creates them runs.
p is a local variable; only its value is a reference, and the variable itself is in the frame.
This is reversed: the local reference is in the frame and the object is on the heap.

q: Two Node objects point to each other through their next fields. Then the only variables that referred to them are set to null. Can they be garbage collected?
options: No: each node still has a reference pointing at it, coming from the other node
Only after the code calls System.gc() for them
Yes: no live variable can reach them, so the cycle does not matter
No: Java objects stay until the program exits
why: The collector starts from live references, such as local variables and static fields, and keeps whatever it can reach. Nothing reachable leads to these two nodes, so both can be freed, even though they refer to each other.
wrong: Counting incoming references is not how reachability works; a cycle with no way in is garbage.
Collection happens on its own; System.gc() is only a hint and is not required.
Unreachable objects are reclaimed while the program runs; that is the point of a garbage collector.

q: For debugging, a service adds every request object to a static List and never removes any. After days, it runs out of memory. Why didn't garbage collection prevent this?
options: The collector skips any object that belongs to a class with a static field
Everything in the list is still reachable, so none of it is garbage
Request objects are too large for the collector to move
Lists are stored outside the heap, where there is no collector
why: A static field lives as long as its class, so the list is always reachable, and so is every request in it. The collector only frees objects that nothing can reach. Holding references you no longer need is the usual Java memory leak.
wrong: Having static fields does not exempt a class's objects; reachability is what counts.
Size does not stop collection; reachable objects are kept and unreachable ones are freed.
Collections and their contents are ordinary heap objects.
